chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Mechanics of Competitive Devaluation

lessons.title: Trade Balances and the J-Curve: Does Devaluation Actually Help Exports?

body.text: A weaker currency does not automatically fix a trade deficit. It can make the deficit worse for months before it gets better, if it gets better at all, and whether it works depends on numbers most currency war headlines never mention: how sensitive buyers and sellers actually are to price.

children.text: The Theory: Why a Weaker Currency Should Help Exports

The textbook logic is simple. A weaker rupee makes Indian goods cheaper for foreign buyers in their own currency, which should raise export volumes, and it makes foreign goods costlier for Indian buyers in rupees, which should reduce import volumes. Both effects should narrow the trade deficit. The catch is the word should: this only works if buyers and sellers actually respond to the price change by enough.

markDefs.definition: The condition that a currency devaluation improves the trade balance only if the sum of the absolute values of export and import price elasticities of demand exceeds 1. If the sum is below 1, a devaluation can actually worsen the trade balance.

children.text: That responsiveness is formalised in the

: the sum of export and import demand elasticities has to exceed 1 for a devaluation to actually improve the trade balance. Below that threshold, the currency effect on prices outweighs the change in quantities, and the trade balance can get worse, not better.

body.latex: |\eta_{exports}| + |\eta_{imports}| > 1 \quad \text{(Marshall-Lerner condition for devaluation to improve the trade balance)}
body.caption: Where η is the price elasticity of demand for exports and imports respectively

body.title: Test the Marshall-Lerner Condition
body.prompt: Country X's export demand elasticity is 0.4 and its import demand elasticity is 0.3. What is the sum of these two elasticities?
body.explanation: 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7, below the threshold of 1. The Marshall-Lerner condition fails here, meaning a devaluation in this scenario would likely worsen Country X's trade balance rather than improve it, since demand on both sides is too price-insensitive to respond enough to offset the currency move.

children.text: The J-Curve: Why It Gets Worse Before It Gets Better

markDefs.definition: The typical short-term path of a country's trade balance after a devaluation: an initial worsening as existing contracts and shipment volumes don't adjust immediately, followed by a gradual improvement over roughly 12 to 24 months as import and export volumes catch up to the new prices, tracing a shape resembling the letter J.

children.text: Even when the Marshall-Lerner condition eventually holds, it rarely holds immediately. Existing import contracts, shipping schedules and buyer relationships were priced and agreed before the devaluation, so in the first few months the same volume of imports simply costs more in rupees while export volumes haven't yet had time to respond to the new, cheaper price. The trade balance actually worsens at first, before elasticities catch up and it improves, a path known as the

body.title: The J-Curve: Trade Balance After a Devaluation (Illustrative)
Quick Check: Where Are We on the J-Curve?
body.question: A country devalues its currency by 10%. Four months later, its trade deficit has actually widened, even though nothing else in the economy has changed. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The devaluation has permanently failed and the trade balance will keep worsening
This is the expected early dip of the J-curve, before import and export volumes have had time to adjust to the new prices
The Marshall-Lerner condition must be exactly equal to 1
The country's currency has actually appreciated, not devalued
body.explanation: Four months is well within the typical early window of a J-curve, where existing contracts and slow-to-adjust volumes mean the trade balance often worsens before it improves. Judging a devaluation's success this early, without waiting the 12 to 24 months elasticities usually need to operate, is a common and costly misreading.

children.text: India's 2013 Test Case: Did Rupee Weakness Actually Narrow the Deficit?

India's current account deficit hit a record high of roughly 4.8% of GDP in FY2012-13, then narrowed sharply to around 1.7% of GDP in FY2013-14, the very year the rupee fell sharply through the taper tantrum covered in the last lesson. On the surface this looks like a clean Marshall-Lerner success story. It wasn't, or at least not purely.

body.text: The government also hiked gold import duty and introduced the 80:20 scheme requiring a fifth of imported gold to be re-exported, directly suppressing India's single largest non-oil import in the same window. Weak domestic growth was separately compressing import demand across the board. Attributing the entire CAD narrowing to rupee-driven export competitiveness alone overstates the currency's role and understates policy intervention and a slowing economy. Real-world trade balance moves are rarely a clean single-cause story, which is exactly the trap this lesson wants you to avoid.

children.text: Why Pass-Through Differs by Sector: IT Services vs Gems and Jewellery

markDefs.definition: How much of a currency move an exporter actually passes on as a change in the foreign-currency price it charges, rather than absorbing it as a change in its own domestic-currency margin.

children.text: The Marshall-Lerner condition assumes exporters actually cut their foreign-currency prices when the rupee weakens. Whether they do depends on

, and it varies enormously by sector. An Indian IT services major billing a long-term US client in dollars rarely cuts its dollar rate just because the rupee weakened; the relationship is sticky, contracts are multi-year, and clients don't switch vendors over small price moves. The rupee's fall shows up almost entirely as a wider rupee margin on the same dollar revenue, not as more billed hours. An analyst checking an IT major's segment-wise revenue mix on screener.in after a rupee depreciation will typically see margin expansion in the next quarter's results, not a jump in export volume.

Gems and jewellery and textile exporters sit at the other end. These are commoditised, price-competitive markets where buyers readily switch suppliers over a few percentage points, so a weaker rupee does genuinely translate into lower dollar quotes and real volume gains, closer to the textbook Marshall-Lerner story.

body.caption: Two Very Different Responses to the Same Rupee Move
headers: What a rupee depreciation mostly does

cells: Low: dollar prices held steady in long-term contracts
Expands rupee margins, does relatively little for export volume
High: prices are competitive and buyers switch easily
Genuinely boosts export volumes, closer to the Marshall-Lerner textbook case

body.title: You Are an Equity Analyst Modelling Two Exporters
body.scenario: The rupee has depreciated 8% against the dollar over the past quarter. You cover two companies: a large IT services exporter with multi-year dollar contracts, and a mid-cap textile exporter selling into price-competitive global markets on relatively short order cycles.
body.prompt: For each company, would you model the rupee move as mostly a margin effect, mostly a volume effect, or some mix of both, and why?
body.modelAnswer: For the IT services exporter, model this almost entirely as a margin effect. Its contracts are typically priced and locked in dollars over multi-year terms, so an 8% rupee depreciation flows through largely unchanged in dollar revenue but boosts EBIT margins meaningfully once translated back to rupees, since a large share of costs (employee costs) are rupee-denominated while revenue stays dollar-denominated. For the textile exporter, model a genuine mix leaning toward volume: in a price-competitive, short-order-cycle market, some of the rupee benefit will likely be passed through as lower dollar quotes to win incremental orders, meaning revenue growth via volume alongside a smaller margin bump than the IT company sees. The practical takeaway for both models: check the segment note or management commentary on pricing strategy post-depreciation before assuming either company automatically gets the full margin windfall.

body.title: State the Condition
body.textWithBlank: The ___ condition says a devaluation only improves the trade balance if the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1.
body.explanation: The Marshall-Lerner condition. Below a combined elasticity of 1, the price effect of a devaluation outweighs the quantity response, and the trade balance can worsen rather than improve.

cards.definition: A devaluation improves the trade balance only if the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1.
The typical path of a trade balance after devaluation: an initial worsening followed by improvement over 12 to 24 months as volumes adjust.
How much of a currency move an exporter passes on as a foreign-currency price change, versus absorbing it as a domestic-currency margin change.
How much export or import volumes change in response to a change in price, the key variable the Marshall-Lerner condition depends on.

points: A devaluation only improves the trade balance if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds: combined export and import demand elasticities must exceed 1.
Even when that condition holds, the trade balance typically worsens first and improves only after 12 to 24 months, the J-curve pattern, because volumes adjust slower than prices.

India's CAD narrowed sharply from FY2012-13 to FY2013-14 alongside the rupee's taper tantrum fall, but gold import curbs and weak domestic demand were significant separate contributors, not currency effects alone.

Pass-through varies sharply by sector: IT services largely convert rupee weakness into margin expansion, while gems, jewellery and textile exporters are more likely to convert it into real volume gains.
Judging whether a devaluation worked requires checking both the time horizon (are you still inside the J-curve dip) and the sector mix (is this an elasticity story or a pass-through story).

This lesson closes the mechanics chapter's currency-and-trade thread; the next lesson turns to how capital flows and the impossible trinity constrain what a country like India can do about any of this in the first place.
